extracted.intended_audience: students of algebraic geometry (Math 216); advanced undergraduates/graduate students learning line bundles and divisors
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook chapter material giving definitions, constructions, and criteria relating line bundles (invertible sheaves), Weil divisors, Cartier divisors, the Picard group and the class group on Noetherian normal schemes, with many exercises and examples. Suitable for learning and applying these concepts to compute Pic and Cl in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of O(n) on projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: The invertible sheaf OPm_k(n) is defined by taking the usual affine cover Ui = Spec k[x0/i, ..., xm/i]/(xi/i − 1) where it is trivial, and using transition functions from Ui to Uj given by x_i/j^n = x_j/i^{-n}. These transition functions satisfy the cocycle condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: O(n) = O(1)^{⊗ n} (with the obvious meaning for negative n via duals). Transition functions are the nth powers of those for O(1); hence O(m) ⊗ O(n) = O(m+n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Global sections of O(n) on P1
rubrics_metrics.description: dim_k Γ(P1_k, O(n)) = n + 1 if n ≥ 0, and 0 otherwise (Exercise 14.1.A / Example computation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete check on standard cover: sections correspond to polynomials of degree ≤ n on one patch matching on overlap, forcing linearity in the n=1 case; more generally identification with homogeneous polynomials gives the dimension count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections of O(n) identified with homogeneous polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections of O(n) on P^m_k are naturally identified with homogeneous degree n polynomials in the m+1 variables (14.1.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification is independent of cover; examples: x+y+2z is a section of O(1) on P^2 and vanishes where the linear form equals 0. Use this dictionary to determine zeros/poles of rational sections of O(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of line bundles on P^m_k
rubrics_metrics.description: For a field k, the O(n) are the only invertible sheaves on P^m_k (statement in 14.1.3 and later: Pic P^n_k ≅ Z generated by O(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 14.1.D gives the P^1 case; later results (14.2.9) show Pic P^n_k ≅ Z with generator O(1), and degree of O(d) is d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Weil divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: A Weil divisor is a formal Z-linear combination of codimension 1 irreducible closed subsets of X: D = ∑ n_Y [Y], with integers n_Y and all but finitely many zero. D is effective if all n_Y ≥ 0. The support is {Y : n_Y ≠ 0}. There are restriction maps Weil X → Weil U for open U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works especially for Noetherian schemes where finite decomposition into irreducible components is available (standing hypothesis for section). On a curve Weil divisors are linear combinations of closed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisor of a rational section (div(s))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an invertible sheaf L and a rational section s not vanishing identically on any component, define div(s) := ∑ val_Y(s) [Y], summing over irreducible codimension‑1 Y, where val_Y(s) is computed by trivializing L near the generic point of Y and taking the valuation of the resulting rational function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: val_Y(s) is well-defined (transition functions are invertible), and val_Y(s) = 0 for all but finitely many Y. This records zeros and poles of the rational section.

rubrics_metrics.name: div homomorphism from (L,s) pairs to Weil X
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment (L, s) (invertible sheaf with nonzero rational section, up to isomorphism) ↦ div(s) defines a group homomorphism {(L, s)}/isom → Weil X (14.2.0.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplication/tensor product of pairs corresponds to addition of divisors; multiplying s by an invertible function gives an isomorphic pair, so div is well-defined on isomorphism classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity of div for normal Noetherian X
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 14.2.1: If X is normal and Noetherian then div : {(L, s)}/isom → Weil X is injective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: if div(L, s) = 0 then s has no poles so is regular; show s gives an isomorphism O_X → L by local trivializations and use normality to assert invertibility of the corresponding rational functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of O_X(D)
rubrics_metrics.description: For irreducible normal X and Weil divisor D define O_X(D) by Γ(U, O_X(D)) := { t ∈ K(X)× : div|_U(t) + D|_U ≥ 0 } ∪ {0} (14.2.2.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections over U are rational functions whose zeros and poles are constrained by D: positive coef in D allows poles of that order, negative coef demands zeros of that order. O_X(D) has a canonical rational section corresponding to 1 (Remark 14.2.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal and locally principal divisors; Prin and LocPrin
rubrics_metrics.description: A Weil divisor D is principal if D = div(f) for some rational function f; principal divisors form Prin X. D is locally principal if covered by opens on which it is principal; these form LocPrin X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If D is principal (and X normal) then O(D) ≅ O. Conversely, if O(D) ≅ O then D is principal (Observation 14.2.5 and Exercise 14.2.G). If D is locally principal then O_X(D) is locally isomorphic to O_X and hence invertible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class group (Cl X) and relation to Pic X
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Cl X := Weil X / Prin X. The map (L,s) ↦ div(s) induces an inclusion Pic X → Cl X (diagram (14.2.7.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More precisely, O(D) gives an element of Pic X when D is locally principal; the diagram summarizes relations among Weil X, LocPrin, Prin, Pic X and Cl X. In many 'reasonable' situations div is an isomorphism onto LocPrin/Prin so Pic X identifies with LocPrin/Prin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard group of affine space / UFD implication
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a unique factorization domain, then Cl(Spec A) = 0, hence Pic(Spec A) = 0 (14.2.8). In particular Cl(A^n_k) = 0 and Pic(A^n_k) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: affine n-space has no nontrivial line bundles in this sense; Quillen–Suslin gives the vanishing of algebraic vector bundles in another sense. Removing closed subsets of codimension >1 doesn't change class groups (excision sequence 14.2.8.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and Pic(P^n_k) ≅ Z
rubrics_metrics.description: For P^n_k the class [Z] of a hyperplane generates Cl P^n_k and Pic P^n_k ≅ Z with generator O(1); define deg O(d) = d (14.2.9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use excision and the identification of affine pieces to see Cl P^n_k is generated by a hyperplane class; O(n) correspond to n times this class and are nontrivial for n ≠ 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial schemes: Pic ≅ Cl (Proposition 14.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is Noetherian and factorial (i.e., every codimension‑1 prime is principal), then for any Weil divisor D, O(D) is invertible, and hence the map Pic X → Cl X is an isomorphism (14.2.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus factoriality (UFD condition) removes the distinction between Weil and Cartier divisors and identifies Pic and Cl.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisting line bundles by divisors (L(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an invertible sheaf L on a normal Noetherian X, define L(D) := O_X(D) ⊗ L (14.2.11). Sections of L(D) are rational sections of L whose zeros and poles are constrained by D: Γ(U, L(D)) := { t rational section of L : div|_U(t) + D|_U ≥ 0 } ∪ {0} (14.2.J).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If D1 and D2 are locally principal, then (O(D1))(D2) ≅ O(D1 + D2). This generalizes the O(D) construction to twisting arbitrary line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Cartier divisors ↔ invertible ideal sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme D ↪ X has ideal sheaf I_D which is invertible iff D is an effective Cartier divisor; equivalently locally cut out by a single non-zerodivisor (8.4.1 / 14.3). The invertible sheaf associated to an effective Cartier divisor is O(D) := I_D^∨, and O(−D) = I_D. There is a canonical section s_D of O(D) cutting out D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locally, if I ≅ A as A-modules generated by a non-zerodivisor a, then multiplication by a gives the closed subscheme; a is unique up to multiplication by a unit (14.3.A). The section s_D cuts out D (14.3.B) and the construction is reversible: a section s of L not locally a zerodivisor cuts out an effective Cartier divisor with O(D) ≅ L (14.3.C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semigroup structure and correspondence of pairs (L,s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Cartier divisors form an abelian semigroup. There is a correspondence between effective Cartier divisors and ordered pairs (L, s) where L is invertible and s is a section not locally a zerodivisor; products of invertible ideal sheaves correspond to sums of divisors and O(D + D') ≅ O(D) ⊗ O(D') (14.3.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This correspondence allows building many invertible sheaves as differences of effective Cartier divisors; in many reasonable circumstances every invertible sheaf arises this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples: Weil divisor not locally principal (cone example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(xy − z^2), let D be the line z = x = 0. Then D is not locally principal, and O_X(D) is not an invertible sheaf; moreover div(x) = 2D (Exercise 14.2.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the stalk at the origin and tangent-space arguments to show non‑principal behavior; shows that Weil divisors need not be Cartier and that O_X(D) can fail to be invertible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q-Cartier and non-Q-Cartier divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: A Weil divisor with a nonzero multiple corresponding to a line bundle is called Q‑Cartier. Examples: some Weil divisors on cones are Q‑Cartier (14.2.Q) while others (e.g., on the cone over the quadric surface) need no multiple to be locally principal, giving non‑Q‑Cartier examples (14.2.R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These distinctions are important in understanding when Weil divisors give rise to line bundles up to torsion; exercises provide concrete constructions and obstructions using affineness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of ideal class group with Cl Spec O_K
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 14.2.S: Identify the ideal class group of the ring of integers O_K in a number field K with the class group Cl(Spec O_K) as defined here, recovering the description of the class group as formal sums of primes modulo principal fractional ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the arithmetic interpretation of the geometric class group and shows how algebraic number theory class groups fit into the Weil/Cl framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: UFD characterization and Nagata's Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 14.2.T: For A a Noetherian integral domain, A is a UFD iff A is integrally closed and Cl(Spec A) = 0. Exercise 14.2.U (Nagata's Lemma): If (x) is prime in A and A[1/x] is a UFD then A is a UFD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criteria and the short exact sequence for class groups (14.2.8.1) to deduce UFD property; Nagata's Lemma gives a practical method for proving UFD via localization.
